opening.headline: When multiple model versions are available, we explore how to manage which version is currently in operation by name and how to separately read the serving resources.
body: We have learned models v1, v2, v3, and only one service is running. If we remember only the version number for the currently operating version, we must update the call code every time we change versions. What we need is a place to manage versions, a label pointing to the currently active version, and a way to decouple the actual serving resources from the model version.

In this class, we first examine how Snowflake Model Registry stores models as schema-level objects and manages them using versions and aliases. Then, we walk through a practical example that demonstrates how to read compute pools and service specifications used when serving models via Snowpark Container Services, including how to determine which alias to read when load is high.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the model versions, aliases, and serving configurations in Snowflake Model Registry.
Version change issues and serving capacity issues can be distinguished at different layers.

screens.title: How to operate model versions in Snowflake
screens.lead: First, let's examine a scenario illustrating the confusion that arises when multiple model versions accumulate. Follow along as we look at the diagram to see which version of the service is being invoked.

visual.alt: A scene showing a question mark placed between the version cards v1, v2, v3 and the service box.
labels: Currently estimated to be in operation
Which version of the service is being called?

paragraphs: After training, there are three models labeled v1, v2, and v3. There is only one service, and which version is currently in operation depends on the memory and notes of a few team members. Every time you want to switch to v3, you must manually update the version number in the code that calls it, and when rolling back, the same process is repeated.

To solve this problem, three components are required: a repository that manages versions, metrics, and metadata in one place; a labeling system that references operational versions by name rather than by number; and a serving infrastructure where the model actually runs. When these three elements are combined, it becomes difficult to distinguish between versioning changes and service scaling operations.

In Snowflake, these three responsibilities are handled by Model Registry, alias, container service, and compute pool respectively. This course covers what each layer is responsible for, and which layer you should examine when issues arise.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Is changing the operating version the same as increasing the load that the service has to handle? In the later case study of the class, we confirm that these two tasks reside at different layers.

screens.outro: Let us consider the concept by comparing it with model registries from other platforms.

screens.title: What is different about a model registry on another platform?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Since you haven't entered an answer yet, first think about the registry you've used before clicking it.

items.prompt: How should a model be stored as an object of a certain unit?
items.answer: In the registry, model objects belong to different schemas. Snowflake Model Registry stores models as first-class objects at the schema level. Therefore, models are placed within databases and schemas, similar to tables or functions, and can be managed with role-based access control.

items.prompt: What is the nameplate for the operating version?
items.answer: Depending on the platform, terms such as alias, stage, or label may differ, but their roles are the same. Instead of using numbers, versions are referenced by names; when a name tag is moved, the calling code retains its original value while only the version it points to changes. In Snowflake, this is referred to as an alias.

items.prompt: Where is the compute environment actually running the model prepared?
items.answer: Putting a model in the registry and serving it are different tasks. In Snowflake, you either call a model method from within the warehouse or serve it via container services on a compute pool of Snowpark Container Services. Distinguishing between these differences is the core of this class.

screens.outro: Based on the comparison above, let's summarize how Snowflake's terminology and concepts correspond to each other.

screens.title: Model Registry: A model is a schema-level object
screens.lead: The following table summarizes the concepts required for model operations, terminology used in Snowflake, and the responsibilities associated with each. Read the rows from top to bottom to verify what each layer is responsible for.

data.caption: Model Operations Concept and Snowflake's Response
rows: The model is stored within the database and schema, and versions, metrics, and metadata are managed together. Access is managed using role-based access control (RBAC).
Version names are used to distinguish and accumulate learning results of the same model. A new version is added using the ADD VERSION clause of ALTER MODEL.

This is a label indicating a specific version. Attach it using the command `ALTER MODEL model_name VERSION version SET ALIAS = name`, and detach it using `UNSET ALIAS`. If the same name is attached to a different version, the label moves to that version.
This is the version used when directly calling methods on the model. The system alias DEFAULT refers to this version.
The methods of logged models can be invoked from a warehouse or served via Snowpark Container Services for GPU-based inference.
data.notes: Common model types such as scikit-learn, xgboost, and PyTorch are natively supported. Models trained using Snowflake ML Functions or Cortex fine-tuned LLMs may not be managed via the registry API.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed the concepts of version and alias, let's examine the operational rules of aliases and the service configuration together.

screens.title: Aliases and serving configurations: nameplate layer and capacity layer
screens.lead: See how moving name tags and configuring serving resources are different tasks.

tabs.label: alias rule
tabs.body: Label a specific version like `ALTER MODEL qa_model VERSION v2 SET ALIAS = PROD;`. An alias must be unique within a model and can be assigned to at most one version. `DEFAULT`, `FIRST`, and `LAST` are system aliases and cannot be used directly. When detached with `UNSET ALIAS` and applied to another version with the same name, the label moves. An alias is not a copy but a label pointing to the original version.

tabs.label: Real-time serving
tabs.body: Real-time inference hosts the model in an HTTP server within Snowpark Container Services, providing a dedicated endpoint. It is suitable when low latency is required, the model serves as the backend for user-facing web or mobile applications, input data is included in an HTTP payload, and horizontal scaling is needed to match traffic fluctuations. It supports automatic scaling, traffic splitting, shadowing, and canary deployments.

tabs.label: Compute pool
tabs.body: A compute pool is a group of VM nodes where services run and is a resource at the account level. When creating a compute pool, you need a machine type instance family, a start node count of `MIN_NODES`, and an upper limit of `MAX_NODES` for scaling. If sudden load spikes are anticipated, you can increase `MIN_NODES` to pre-provision nodes and avoid waiting for automatic scaling. `MAX_NODES` helps prevent excessive node scaling by automatic expansion, thus keeping costs under control.

tabs.label: Service Specification
tabs.body: The service specification is in YAML format and contains the settings passed to Snowflake when creating a service. It defines the container name, image, environment variables, resource requests and limits, readiness probe, and liveness endpoint. The resource `requests` specifies the amount to be allocated, and `limits` specifies the upper limit that will not be exceeded. The default value for the readiness probe `periodSeconds` is 5, and the default value for the liveness probe `failureThreshold` is 3.

tabs.label: Required permissions
tabs.body: Model serving operates within Snowpark Container Services, therefore the account must have USAGE or OWNERSHIP permissions on the compute pool where the service runs. To create a public endpoint, the account must have BIND SERVICE ENDPOINT permissions, as well as OWNER or READ permissions on the model.

screens.outro: Now we will directly read SQL and YAML to verify what each line defines.

screens.title: Code Reading: alias change, compute pool, service specification
screens.lead: Read the following code from top to bottom. The right-side description indicates the symptoms that occur when there is a mismatch between the explanation and the respective section. The reading order is: label, node limit, container settings.

data.code:
ALTER MODEL qa_model VERSION v2 SET ALIAS = PROD;

CREATE COMPUTE POOL qa_pool
  MIN_NODES = 1
  MAX_NODES = 3
  INSTANCE_FAMILY = CPU_X64_XS;

spec:
  containers:
  - name: model-server
    image: /qa_db/public/repo/model-server:latest
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: 4G
        cpu: 1
      limits:
        memory: 8G
        cpu: 2
    readinessProbe:
      port: 8080
      path: /health
  endpoints:
  - name: predict
    port: 8080

notes.note: In v2, attach the PROD label. If PROD was already attached to a previous version, the label is moved to v2. Using system alias names such as DEFAULT, FIRST, or LAST will not work.

MIN_NODES is the number of nodes initially provisioned in the pool, MAX_NODES is the upper limit for auto-scaling, and INSTANCE_FAMILY refers to the machine type of the nodes. If MAX_NODES is too small, the system will not add nodes even under heavy load, resulting in delayed responses.
Specify the name and image of the container to be executed. The service will not start if the image path is incorrect.

Requests are the resources being acquired, and limits are the upper bounds that must not be exceeded. If the limit is smaller than the model's requirements, the service may become unstable or restart.

Readiness check. Verify whether the service is ready to receive requests by accessing the /health endpoint. If the path or port differs from the actual server, the service will remain in an uninitialized state.
This is the service endpoint and port. Read it together with the probe's port to verify that they match.

screens.outro: Since we've learned the order in which to read code, let's apply this order to a single example.

screens.title: Case Explanation: When aliases are moved, leading to overload
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down a case where responses lag after an alias is moved, step by step. Follow the next arrow to see which layer you should read.

visual.alt: PROD alias arrow moves from v1 to v2, and the diagram shows a change in the number of compute pool nodes below.

steps.title: Context: PROD alias exists in v1
steps.body: The PROD alias is attached to v1, and the service invokes the model based on PROD. We have now added v2 to the registry. Currently, since only the addition has been made, PROD still points to v1, so there is no impact on the service.

steps.title: Step 1 Move: Move the label to v2
steps.body: When you move the label to `ALTER MODEL qa_model VERSION v2 SET ALIAS = PROD;`, the code that calls based on alias will automatically use v2 without any modifications. To revert, use the same command to attach PROD back to v1.

steps.title: Stage 2 Distinction: Registry Modification and Service Reflection
steps.body: Alias migration involves changes within the registry. It is necessary to check separately in the service configuration to determine when the container service reflects a new version. Moving a name does not simultaneously change the service's capacity or settings.

steps.title: Step 3: Read Settings: Read Compute Pool Line
steps.body: The service pool is constructed as follows: `CREATE COMPUTE POOL qa_pool MIN_NODES = 1 MAX_NODES = 1 INSTANCE_FAMILY = CPU_X64_XS;` has both start node count and upper limit set to 1. The machine type is the smallest CPU family.

steps.title: Stage 4 symptom: Response continues to lag
steps.body: Immediately after the v2 update, traffic congestion caused delayed responses, and the number of nodes remained stagnant at one. While it may seem plausible that the new model is flawed, the observation that node count does not increase points in a different direction.

steps.title: Step 5 cause: The limit equals the initial value.
steps.body: If MAX_NODES is equal to the initial value, automatic scaling has no room to increase. Even if the load increases, the cluster will scale down to just one node. The root cause was not related to the version but rather to the service capacity tier.

steps.title: Step 6 Adjustment: Modify the initial values and upper bounds.
steps.body: Based on the expected load, increase `MIN_NODES` to prepare for surges, and raise `MAX_NODES` to three to keep costs under control. Then, together, review whether the service specifications `requests`, `limits`, and `readinessProbe` are compatible with the new version. If the new version requires more memory, the limits must also be adjusted.

steps.title: Conclusion: Read layer by layer.
steps.body: Version upgrades involve the registry's alias, while scaling is managed by the compute pool and service specifications. Since these are separate layers, issues must be addressed independently. Assuming the upgrade is complete merely by moving the alias will cause overlooking issues such as the load problem in this case.

screens.outro: We have organized the case study; now I will conclude by summarizing the core concepts.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: The concepts are the same; only the terminology differs.
screens.lead: Summarize the core of the lecture. Read through it, matching each term you use in your platform with its corresponding term.

paragraphs: Model operations consist of four elements regardless of the platform: model object, version, operation alias, and serving resources. In Snowflake, a model is a schema-level object; new learning results are accumulated as versions; operation aliases point to versions; and serving is managed by container services on a compute pool.

When a problem occurs, you must first determine which layer the issue resides in. Whether an alias is being called is determined by the alias, whether the service can withstand load is determined by the compute pool's `MIN_NODES` and `MAX_NODES`, and whether the container is running stably is determined by the service specification's resources and probes. The fact that automatic scaling has no room to increase when MAX_NODES equals its initial value can only be discovered by reading the configuration line.
Finally, simply registering a model in the registry does not start serving. Serving requires a separate service instance and a compute pool, along with the appropriate permissions.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Changing an alias is about altering which version is referenced, while adjusting a compute pool is about changing how much capacity it can handle. Verify both actions separately.

checks.intro: Interpret the settings you just read directly. The results are not recorded.
checks.q:
There was a sudden increase in load in the compute pool, but no additional nodes were added. What is the most likely cause?  
CREATE COMPUTE POOL qa_pool MIN_NODES = 1 MAX_NODES = 1 INSTANCE_FAMILY = CPU_X64_XS;
options: Because the INSTANCE_FAMILY is small, the alias cannot be migrated to the new version.
MAX_NODES is equal to MIN_NODES, so automatic scaling has no room to increase.
The PROD alias remains in v1, preventing node creation.
If MIN_NODES is 1, the service does not start.
checks.explain: MAX_NODES is the upper limit of nodes that can be automatically scaled up. If set equal to the initial value, no additional nodes can be added even during sudden load spikes, and to provide headroom, either MIN_NODES should be increased or the upper limit should be raised.

wrong.0: INSTANCE_FAMILY is a node machine type and is unrelated to alias migration.
wrong.2: An alias is merely a label within the registry and has no relation to node creation.
wrong.3: MIN_NODES must be a value greater than 0, and 1 is a valid value.

checks.intro: Please follow the procedure in order. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Please consider the procedure for promoting a new version using alias in the correct order.
items: Move the label of the model to v2 by setting SET ALIAS = PROD in ALTER MODEL.
Check the service configuration to see when the service reflects the new version.
Check whether the compute pool capacity and resource limits are sufficient in the new version.
checks.explain: You must first add the version, then move the label, and afterward verify the reflection timestamp and resource availability.

glossary.def: Snowflake feature that stores and manages model versions, metrics, and metadata as schema-level objects.
This is a label indicating a specific model version. If the same label is attached to a different version, the label moves to that version.
A group of VM nodes on which Snowpark Container Services runs, a resource at the account level.
YAML configuration defining container images, resources, probes, and endpoints.
This is Snowflake's environment running services and model serving based on containers.

misconceptions.myth: An alias is a copy of a model version.
misconceptions.fact: An alias is not a copy but a label pointing to the existing version. Moving the label does not change the version itself.

misconceptions.myth: Compute pools and warehouses are the same resource.
misconceptions.fact: A compute pool is a resource for container services and serves as a account-level component similar to a warehouse. The serving capacity is determined by the node limit of the compute pool.

misconceptions.myth: Once a model is uploaded to the registry, it is automatically served.
misconceptions.fact: Registry entry is about storage and management. To serve via container service, you need a separate compute pool, service creation, and required permissions.

misconceptions.myth: Moving only the alias completes the operational transition.
misconceptions.fact: You must read together when the service reflects a new version, and whether the pool's node limits and service specifications' resources and probes are compatible with the new version.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The concepts of model object, version, operating nameplate, and serving resources are the same, differing only in terminology across platforms.
In Snowflake, a model is a schema-level object managed through versioning and alias.
A compute pool is a resource that hosts services, and service specifications are container configurations.
If MAX_NODES is equal to the initial value, automatic scaling has no room to increase, so it reads the configuration line for verification.
